points.description: Purpose: both provide broadcasting that is more efficient than flooding, i.e. they reduce/minimise duplicate packets in the network.
points.partial_credit: Says only that they are used for broadcasting, without the idea of fewer duplicates/better than flooding.

points.description: Reverse Path Forwarding: using the unicast routing table, a node X receiving a packet from source S via neighbour N forwards it to all other neighbours (not back to N) only if X would send packets to S via N (i.e. the packet arrived on the best path back to S); otherwise it discards it.
points.partial_credit: Mentions checking the path/routing table toward the source but omits the condition on N or the forwarding to all other neighbours.

points.description: Reverse Path Broadcast: works like RPF but forwards only on edges that are part of a spanning tree; nodes learn which trees they belong to by monitoring unicast traffic (X is on the best path between A and B if it sees unicast packets between them).
points.partial_credit: States it is RPF restricted to spanning-tree edges, or the traffic-monitoring idea, but not both.

rubric.notes: Full marks need the purpose (fewer duplicates than flooding), how RPF decides to forward (route back to the source goes via the incoming neighbour), and how RPB differs (only spanning-tree edges, learned from unicast traffic). Give part marks for half-stated or vague mechanisms. A general statement like "they broadcast packets" with no mechanism earns about half at most; wrong mechanisms earn nothing for that point.
